strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing nested/Matryoshka ViTs (HydraViT, MatFormer, SortedNet, DynaBERT) allocate fixed compute per input, and ThinkingViT introduces input-adaptive compute allocation within a nested backbone without a separate router. The routing-free design (entropy-based 'aha' criterion) is elegant and avoids the redundancy the authors correctly identify in MoE-style routing for image-level decisions.

The core mechanism (Token Recycling, Eq. 3) is simple, well-motivated, and supported by strong empirical evidence. The ablations are unusually thorough: Appendix C compares five alternative conditioning strategies (layerwise snapshots, memory tokens), Appendix D compares six fusion strategies and α initializations, and Table 1 convincingly shows that naive recursion and depth expansion plateau or degrade, justifying the progressive width expansion.

Evaluation breadth is good: ImageNet-1K plus V2, ReaL, R, A, and Sketch; throughput and GMACs Pareto curves (Figures 2-4, 7, 12); comparisons against both nested baselines, early exit (Appendix B: +3.36 p.p. over a matched early-exit baseline), and token-level dynamic models like ToMe, DynamicViT, MoD (Appendix F). Gains are consistent rather than isolated to one benchmark.

The load-distribution analysis (Figure 8) and entropy distribution analysis (Figure 5) directly validate the central claim that entropy-based halting allocates compute sensibly. The limitations section (Section 4.5, Appendix J) is honest and specific, e.g., the observed collapse of efficiency on uniformly hard inputs (ImageNet-A) and the 'jumping too far' effect in head expansion.
The backbone-preserving design makes the method a plugin upgrade for pretrained ViTs, which increases practical usefulness.
weaknesses: Scale of experiments is limited. All headline results are built on DeiT-Tiny with a doubled 24-layer backbone (~22M params). Appendix G offers a DeiT-Small-based comparison but it is presented only as a figure without the detailed analysis given to the tiny model. There is no evidence the approach scales to DeiT-Base/Large or ViT-B/g, no transfer to downstream tasks (detection/segmentation), and no LLM experiments despite the conclusion claiming the principle is architecture-agnostic. For a method whose pitch is elastic inference across heterogeneous hardware, this is a meaningful gap.

The comparison fairness needs more scrutiny. ThinkingViT uses 24 layers while the Table 1 depth-expanded control achieves only 77.35 at 24 layers; however, it is not fully clear whether all baselines in Figure 2 use the same depth/parameter budget or were trained with identical epochs and preprocessing. The 'up to 2.0/2.9 p.p.' claims are cherry-picked maxima from Pareto curves, and there is no reporting of seed variance or statistical significance despite ~100 training runs mentioned during prototyping.

Conceptual novelty is moderate. The method is essentially HydraViT-style head nesting + confidence-based early exit (a well-established technique, cited as such) + a learned additive fusion of first-pass tokens. Each ingredient exists in prior work; the contribution is their combination and the empirical demonstration that width-progressive rethinking beats depth-based early exit and naive recursion. This is a legitimate contribution but incremental.

The practical benefit of elastic inference is understated in the results: at the default full-compute setting ThinkingViT uses 5.85 GMACs for 81.44%, but the entropy-threshold sweep (Table 4) shows accuracy drops steeply below ~3.5 GMACs (e.g., 74.7% at 1.44 GMACs), and on hard distributions (ImageNet-R/A) nearly all samples trigger the second stage, negating the efficiency advantage. The practical operating range where ThinkingViT is both efficient and accurate is narrower than the abstract implies.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned; some training details (λ_i values actually used, α learned value only given in an ablation appendix, projection-layer details) are scattered or absent. The appendix ablations (Table 6) used a different training regime than the main results, which the authors acknowledge, slightly weakening the comparability of that evidence.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., Section 3.3 discusses sandwich rule and stochastic sampling without stating which was used for final models; some claims like 'surpasses nested baselines by up to 2.0 p.p.' would be better anchored to specific operating points).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine limitation of nested/Matryoshka ViTs (fixed compute per input) and the proposed combination of head-level nesting with entropy-based progressive inference is a sensible, well-motivated design; the Token Recycling mechanism (Eq. 3) is a simple way to make the second pass condition on the first rather than routing to a discarded decision.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: ImageNet-1K plus V2/ReaL/R/A/Sketch variants, comparisons against multiple nested baselines (MatFormer, HydraViT, SortedNet, DynaBERT) and token-level dynamic models (ToMe, DynamicViT, MoD, A-MoD), and an early-exit comparison (+3.36 p.p. at matched GMACs, Appendix B).

Ablations are thorough: fusion strategy comparison (Table 7), recycling variants including layerwise snapshots and memory tokens (Table 6), loss weighting (Table 2), multi-stage variants (Table 3), and threshold sweep (Table 4).

The paper is honest about limitations: degraded efficiency on uniformly hard inputs (Section 4.5, Figure 7), training overhead, and aggressive expansion jumps (Appendix J), which increases trust in the reported results.
The negative results in Table 1 (naive recursion and depth expansion plateau or degrade) are useful evidence motivating width-progressive expansion over depth- or iteration-based alternatives.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the architecture slices (embeddings, heads, MLP, NORM) are directly inherited from HydraViT, the certainty-based halting is standard confidence-based early exit/cascade deferral, and the contribution reduces to (i) applying early exit to a nested ViT along the width dimension and (ii) a projection-plus-learnable-scalar fusion (Eq. 3). The technical machinery is thin relative to the framing.

Parameter comparability across models is unclear and potentially favorable to the proposed method: ThinkingViT has 22.01M parameters vs. DeiT-Tiny's 5.7M initial checkpoint, and Table 1 lists it at depth 24 with 22.1M parameters. It is not sufficiently specified whether baselines in Figure 2 are matched in parameter count and depth; the claimed 2.0/2.9 p.p. gains at matched throughput/GMACs could partly reflect a larger model.

All results are at a single small scale (DeiT-Tiny base, 224x224, 3->6 heads), with DeiT-Small-based baselines only in Appendix G. The elastic-inference claims for 'heterogeneous hardware' and the architecture-agnostic/LLM claims in the conclusion are not supported by any experiments at other scales or on other architectures.

The 'thinking' framing borrowed from reasoning LLMs is mostly marketing; there is no analysis of what the second round learns, why attention-head expansion specifically (vs. MLP width or depth) matters, and the entropy criterion is acknowledged as performing merely 'on par' with more complex criteria.

Practical deployment concerns are underexamined: two-pass inference with a data-dependent exit complicates batching and real-world latency; throughput is only measured on an A100, and the effect of the second-round call ratio (71.7% at threshold 0.1, Table 4) on realistic serving is not discussed.
No code or training-recipe release is stated, and with roughly 100 training runs of 300 epochs used for tuning, reproducibility of the exact operating points in Figure 2 is a concern.

The throughput gain claim in the abstract ('up to 2.0 p.p. at the same throughput') rests on picking specific points on Pareto curves; per-point comparisons and confidence/variance over seeds are not reported.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: combining Matryoshka-style nested architectures with input-adaptive compute allocation. The paper convincingly identifies the gap (nested models use fixed compute per input; MoE-style routers are too weak for image-level difficulty estimation) and addresses it without a separate router.

The Token Recycling mechanism is a sensible and novel design: rather than discarding the first-round computation, tokens are fused back into the input via a learnable projection scaled by α, yielding a genuinely input-conditional pipeline. The ablations in Appendices C and D (activation snapshots, memory tokens, six fusion strategies, α initialization) are thorough and support the design choices.

Empirical results are strong relative to the evaluated baselines: up to 2.0 p.p. at equal throughput and 2.9 p.p. at equal GMACs on ImageNet-1K, with consistent gains on ImageNet-V2, -ReaL, -R, -A, and -Sketch, and favorable comparison to DeiT-Base (81.44% with 22.1M params vs. 86.6M). Appendix B shows a +3.36 p.p. advantage over a matched early-exit baseline.

Evaluation of the routing mechanism is convincing: entropy distributions across ImageNet variants (Fig. 5), load/accuracy distribution across thresholds (Fig. 8), and prediction dynamics across rounds (Fig. E) directly support the claim that entropy-based halting works as intended.

The paper is refreshingly honest about limitations: degradation on uniformly hard inputs (Section 4.5, ImageNet-A), training overhead, and 'jumping too far' between stages are explicitly discussed rather than hidden.

Naive-recursion and depth-expansion experiments (Table 1) justify the core architectural claim that progressive width expansion (more heads) is necessary, rather than merely recycling with a fixed network.
weaknesses: Limited model scale: all main results are built on DeiT-Tiny initialization at 224x224, and no experiments at DeiT-Small/Higher-capacity ThinkingViT scale or higher-resolution regimes are shown for the proposed method itself. It remains unclear whether the gains persist at larger scales where nested/elastic inference matters most in practice.

Potential confound in headline comparisons: ThinkingViT (22.1M params, 5.85 GMACs at full capacity) is substantially larger than the DeiT-Tiny initialization of the baselines, and its full model is larger than DeiT-Small (4.6 GMACs). The paper does report DeiT-Small in Appendix B/G, which helps, but the main-figure narrative of beating all baselines could be stated with more care about parameter/GMAC parity; a same-budget, non-nested strong model (e.g., finetuned DeiT-Small at 5.85 GMACs) is not a central comparison.

Statistical rigor is thin: results appear to be single-seed; approximately 100 training runs are mentioned but no error bars, seed variance, or significance tests are reported for the 2.0-2.9 p.p. margins, which are meaningful but not enormous.

Training cost is roughly doubled by joint execution of all thinking rounds (acknowledged in Appendix J), yet no end-to-end train-time or energy accounting is provided against simply training separate models; the efficiency argument is thus primarily inference-side.

Generalization scope: evaluation is confined to the ImageNet family; no transfer tasks, downstream fine-tuning, or downstream dense-prediction evaluations, so the practical utility beyond classification robustness variants is not established.

Reproducibility: no code release or repository is mentioned, and several important details (λi values chosen for the final model, exact training schedule for the 3H->6H final configuration, threshold τ selection protocol) are underspecified in the main text.

Two-stage formulation in practice: despite the general n-stage presentation, all headline results use two stages (with a third stage adding accuracy only at large GMAC cost); the framing as 'progressive thinking stages' slightly overstates what is empirically validated.

Minor presentation issues: Fig. 2/4 curves are hard to read precisely; Table 4 shows a non-monotonic anomaly in second-round call ratio (71.7 at τ=0.1 vs. 70.58 at τ=0.3) that is unexplained and could indicate measurement or reporting error.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: combining nested (Matryoshka-style) ViTs with input-adaptive compute allocation via confidence-based early exit is a natural but non-trivial combination, and the paper articulates why naive token-level routers and naive looping of the same model (Table 1) are insufficient.

The Token Recycling mechanism (Eq. 4) is simple, well-described, and empirically validated: the appendix ablations (Tables 4 and 5) carefully compare alternative conditioning strategies (layerwise snapshots, memory tokens, KV-cache reuse) and fusion/projection variants, supporting the design choice rather than asserting it.

Breadth of evaluation is strong for an efficiency paper: ImageNet-1K plus V2/ReaL/R/A/Sketch, throughput and GMACs on A100, extension to Swin, downstream semantic segmentation (ADE20K, Cityscapes), comparisons to both width-based (MatFormer, HydraViT, DynaBERT, SortedNet) and depth-based (BranchyNet, PABEE, BERxiT, ViT-EE, etc.) baselines, and a demonstration of complementarity with token pruning (Fig. 14).

Honest analysis of failure modes and trade-offs: e.g., 3H→12H costs 23.41 GMACs for only 0.91 p.p. gain (Sec. 4.2), the ~2% of samples that get worse after the second round (Appendix F), training overhead of nested models, and the 'jumping too far' limitation (Appendix I).
Batched inference (Algorithm 1) and calibration of throughput via per-image timing on the full validation set show the method is practically deployable, not just a GMACs accounting trick.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea is essentially HydraViT-style head slicing plus a standard confidence/entropy early-exit gate (well established since BranchyNet/PABEE) plus a learned scalar fusion of the first-round embeddings. Each ingredient exists; the contribution is their integration and tuning, which is somewhat incremental for a top-tier venue.

Potential unfairness in the training setup: ThinkingViT is initialized from a pretrained DeiT-Tiny checkpoint (Sec. 4.1), while baselines are described only as 'trained following the training recipes in [41]'. If baselines are trained from scratch under the DeiT recipe while ThinkingViT starts from pretrained weights, part of the reported 2.0–2.9 p.p. advantage could come from initialization rather than the method. The paper should either fine-tune all methods from the same checkpoint or train all from scratch; this ambiguity undermines the headline claims.

Absolute performance is modest: the best configuration reaches 81.44% top-1 with 5.85 GMACs, which trails modern ViTs of similar cost; all comparisons are within a DeiT-Tiny-based ecosystem, so the practical significance of the gains is not fully established.

The 'up to X p.p.' claims are pointwise maxima along threshold-swept curves, which can flatter the method; the operating-point advantage over baselines is smaller in much of the plotted range, and the entropy threshold τ must be swept per deployment, whereas baselines offer multiple nested subnetworks with no such tuning.

Latency semantics are under-discussed: throughput improves because easy samples exit early, but hard samples incur a full second pass plus rebatching; mean per-sample latency and tail latency on mixed workloads are not reported, and the throughput measurements use a batch size of 512 that is unrealistic for the edge-deployment scenarios motivating the paper.

Several quantitative details are inconsistent or unclear: the GMACs formula in Sec. 4.1 sums over an index i that also denotes samples (notational sloppiness); the second-round call ratio changes non-monotonically between thresholds 0.1 and 0.3 in Table 3 (71.7% vs. 70.58%) with nearly identical accuracy, which deserves explanation; the learned α = −0.19 (negative recycling weight) is surprising and unexplained.
No explicit statement of code release, which, combined with ~100 training runs of 300 epochs each, makes exact reproduction of the reported trade-off curves difficult.

The 'thinking'/'aha moment' framing borrowed from LLM reasoning (DeepSeek-R1, o1) is largely cosmetic; the mechanism is a two-round coarse-to-fine classifier, and the framing risks overstating what the method does.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper reports results on ImageNet-1K plus five robustness variants (V2, ReaL, R, A, Sketch), semantic segmentation on ADE20K and Cityscapes via Segmenter, an extension to Swin, comparisons against both width-nested (MatFormer, HydraViT, SortedNet, DynaBERT) and depth-based early-exit baselines (SDN, PABEE, BERxiT, ViT-EE, PCEE, LGViT, BranchyNet), and combinations with token pruning. This breadth of evaluation exceeds the typical standard for efficiency-oriented architecture papers.

The ablation material is unusually thorough: six fusion strategies (Table 5), alternative recycling designs including memory tokens, KV-cache reuse, and layerwise snapshots (Table 4), entropy-threshold sweeps with call ratios (Table 3), multi-round configurations (Tables 6-7), and a prediction-dynamics analysis (Fig. 13). Appendix H also isolates the comparison on a common DeiT-Small backbone, mitigating backbone confounds.

The core mechanism is well-motivated and empirically supported: combining width-nested subnetworks with input-adaptive early exit fills a real gap, since existing nested models use a fixed compute budget per input. Table 1 (naive looping) and Fig. 7 (load distribution and accuracy of early exits) give direct evidence for the two design claims, and the throughput-vs-GMACs curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 15) show consistent dominance over baselines at matched budgets rather than cherry-picked points.

The paper is largely reproducible: implementation in timm with a public training recipe, hardware and batch-size specifications for throughput measurements, an explicit GMACs averaging formula, batched inference pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and clear documentation of the learned scalar alpha and its initialization.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental. The nested architecture is directly inherited from HydraViT (the paper itself says 'Inspired by [14]'), confidence/entropy-based early exit is a standard technique, and Token Recycling reduces to a single learnable scalar alpha times a linear projection of first-pass tokens added to input embeddings (Eq. 4), with an ablation showing padding/repetition variants perform within ~1 p.p. of the chosen method. The contribution is a sensible combination of existing ingredients rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the 'thinking'/'aha moment' framing overstates what is a two-pass confidence-thresholded forward pass.

A potential fairness concern in the baseline comparison is not fully addressed: ThinkingViT is 'initialized with a pretrained DeiT-Tiny checkpoint' (Sec. 4.1), while it is stated only that baselines follow the training recipes of [41]. If baselines were trained from scratch or under a different initialization regime, part of the reported 2.0-2.9 p.p. advantage could stem from initialization rather than the method. The paper should clarify initialization for all baselines or include a from-scratch ablation.

The practical latency benefit depends on batch rebatching behavior (Algorithm 1): throughput is measured at batch size 512 with batch shrinking across rounds, but the synchronization and shrinking batch effects at deployment-relevant batch sizes, and the interaction of the two sequential passes with hardware, are not analyzed beyond the aggregate throughput curve. Additionally, the Table 1 'naive iteration' argument is based on a single model/one configuration, which is thin support for the claim that capacity expansion (rather than better fusion) drives the gains.

The mechanism is fragile to configuration choices: 3H->6H is best, but 3H->12H costs 4x compute for 0.9 p.p. gain and 2H->3H drops to 74.1%, and the authors note 'jumping too far reduces effectiveness' (Appendix I). This narrow operating window, combined with ~100 training runs of 300 epochs during prototyping, suggests substantial tuning cost that is acknowledged only as a generic nested-model limitation; the true training budget versus baselines is unclear.

Only two rounds are used in practice (three-round variants underperform at their compute levels), the method is evaluated mainly on small models (DeiT-Tiny/Small scale, Swin-S), and section references contain errors (e.g., Sec. 4.2 routing, Sec. 4.7 depth baselines vs. early-exit ordering in Sec. 4 intro), which weakens clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: existing nested/Matryoshka Transformers (MatFormer, HydraViT, SortedNet, DynaBERT) allocate a fixed compute budget per input, and ThinkingViT adds input-adaptive computation via entropy-gated progressive head expansion without a separate router. The design question (Section 1) is well motivated.

Empirical results are convincing and broad: up to 2.0 p.p. accuracy gains at equal throughput and 2.9 p.p. at equal GMACs against recent strong baselines (NeurIPS'20–'24) on ImageNet-1K, with consistent wins on ImageNet-V2/-ReaL/-R/-A/-Sketch (Fig. 4, 11, 12).

The evaluation goes beyond classification: plug-in transfer to semantic segmentation via Segmenter on ADE20K and Cityscapes (Fig. 9-10), extension to the hierarchical Swin backbone (Fig. 8a), comparison with depth-based early-exit models (Fig. 8b), and complementarity with token pruning (Appendix G, Fig. 14). This breadth strengthens the generality claims.
Table 1 provides a useful motivating experiment showing naive iteration of the same model saturates in vision, justifying progressive capacity expansion.

Ablations are thorough: token-recycling design variants (Table 4), fusion/projection strategies and α initialization (Table 5), entropy-threshold sweeps with load distribution (Table 3, Fig. 7), attention-expansion and loss-weighting combinations (Table 6), and three-stage hierarchies (Table 7). Prediction dynamics (Appendix F, Fig. 13) honestly report ~2% overthinking cases.

Limitations are candidly discussed in Appendix I (training overhead of nested architectures, effectiveness of gradual vs. aggressive expansion), and the mechanism is clearly specified (Eqs. 4-6, Algorithm 1), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the method is essentially a combination of existing ingredients — HydraViT-style nested head slicing, entropy-based early halting, and a residual-like fusion of previous-round embeddings into input embeddings (Eq. 4). The 'thinking'/'aha moment' framing borrowed from LLM reasoning overstates the mechanism, which is a two-stage width-expansion early-exit scheme.

The Token Recycling gain over the natural alternative (a flat 6-head model, i.e., DeiT-Small at 79.9% vs. 81.44%) is the core claim, but the ablation table for recycling variants (Table 4) was trained with a stochastic, not the final joint, training strategy, making exact attribution of the +1.5 p.p. over the flat baseline less rigorous.

Evaluation is limited to DeiT-Tiny/Small scale (~22M params); no results on larger backbones (ViT-B/L, modern architectures beyond Swin-S) to confirm the approach scales, and the comparison baselines all share the same backbone rather than comparing against the strongest independently-trained dynamic models.

The elastic operating range is obtained by sweeping the entropy threshold post-hoc on the validation set; the paper does not discuss how τ should be selected for a new deployment distribution, where entropy miscalibration under distribution shift could degrade the routing quality.

A second full forward pass over the entire backbone for uncertain inputs may be latency-unfriendly compared to depth early-exit approaches on sequential hardware; the paper reports throughput on an A100 with batched inference (Appendix J) but not single-image latency.
No explicit statement of code release, and roughly 100 training runs of 300 epochs each suggests substantial compute for hyperparameter exploration, which may limit reproducibility for other groups.

Minor presentation issues: some claims ('performs on par with more complex criteria [22]') lack supporting detail in the main text; Figure 1 caption's claims rely on visual inspection of curves rather than tabulated numbers at matched operating points in the main paper.
